deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations. It is not in Riemann's hand. It is the second page (verso) of a letter dated Kerstlingerode bei Göttingen, 9 September 1875.

The writer is almost certainly Karl Hattendorff, who in 1867 edited Riemann's posthumous memoir 'Über die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung' (Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 13) from Riemann's manuscript and oral explanations. The recipient ('Geehrtester Herr College') is almost certainly Heinrich Weber, then preparing Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876). The letter accompanies Hattendorff's revised version of the minimal-surface memoir for that edition.

Content of this page:

(1) Notation. Hattendorff defends keeping the word 'Argument' for the coefficient of i in the logarithm of a complex quantity. In modern terms that is arg z = Im(log z), so log z = log|z| + i·arg z. He says the term comes from Riemann himself: in his lectures Riemann 'stets' (always) used this expression and no other, and he also used it in the explanations he gave Hattendorff about the manuscript (M.S.). He therefore proposes not to change it.

(2) 'Historische Einleitung'. The introduction was meant only as a broad overview of earlier work, not an exhaustive historical-critical treatise. It is already long and could be dropped from the new printing. In case Weber wants to keep it, Hattendorff has completed it.

(3) Poisson's note. Hattendorff remarks that Poisson's note stresses the main question: whether, for a given contour, the arbitrary functions in the general solution of the minimal-surface equation can be determined. Poisson restricted himself to a contour lying only infinitesimally out of the plane. Hattendorff thinks this restriction was introduced only to simplify the problem.
- Mathematical content (my gloss, not on the page): if z = εw(x,y) with ε small, the minimal-surface equation (1+z_y^2) z_xx − 2 z_x z_y z_xy + (1+z_x^2) z_yy = 0 reduces at first order to Laplace's equation w_xx + w_yy = 0. Poisson's question then becomes a Dirichlet problem for harmonic functions.
- Since Poisson never published the promised detailed account, his note seems to have had no influence on later treatments of the problem.

The next page continues with Enneper, Weierstrass, Schwarz, and an error on p. 14 of the first printing.
errors: The claim that the term 'Argument' (for the angle or imaginary part of the logarithm) originates with Riemann is historically doubtful. Cauchy was already using 'argument' in this sense in the 1840s (e.g. Exercices d'analyse et de physique mathématique). At most, Riemann used and popularized the term in German; Hattendorff's attribution is probably inaccurate.
No mathematical derivations appear on the page, so there are no computational errors to check.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editorial letter by Hattendorff, not a Riemann manuscript, and contains no mathematics. Its only historically interesting detail is the testimony that Riemann always used the word 'Argument' in lectures. That is a minor point of terminology, and the attribution of the term's origin to Riemann is likely wrong, since Cauchy used it earlier.

checkable.asserts: The 'Argument' is the coefficient of i in the (principal) logarithm: Im(log z) = arg z.
